INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
America First Legal Foundation (AFL) is a
nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting the
rule of law in the United States by ensuring due
process and equal protection for every American
citizen, and encouraging understanding of the law
and individual rights guaranteed under the
Constitution and laws of the United States.
AFL has a substantial interest in this case.
Ensuring that States can prosecute criminal offenders
without suffering extra -constitutional burdens
promotes citizens’ safety , supports federalism, and
reinforces the rule of law . And constitutionalizing
rules beyond the law’s original meaning based on
purported social-science consensus is troubling —
especially when that “consensus” disregards on -theground evidence.*


* No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no person other than amic us curiae, its members,  or its
counsel made a monetary contribution to its preparation or
submission.

2


SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Constitution is silent about how many jurors
sit on a jury. Significant evidence shows that “ jury,”
in both 1791 and 1868, named an institution  that
functioned to check the government —not a number.
Because the jury’s core meaning lies in its function,
Petitioner’s claim is testable.
Petitioner says that “a six -person jury” is “more
likely to rule against a criminal defendant than a jury
of 12.” Pet. Br. 30. Yet Petitioner and his amici rely on
decades-old research that generally did not focus on
outcome differences between six - and twelve -person
juries. This brief presents a new empirical analysis of
jury outcomes in Florida and in States that mostly use
larger juries. This analysis casts doubt on Petitioner’s
claim that Florida’s six -person juries disadvantage
criminal defendants.
First, Florida’s six-person juries consistently check
prosecutors. Over the last five fiscal years, about
27.7% of noncapital Florida prosecutions failed before
a jury, by acquittal or dismissal —a figure that never
moved more than a point and a half. The larger -jury
States do no better  on similar measures . New York
acquits in about one felony verdict in five; Washington
and Texas land in the same range.
Second, the evidence does not show that Florida’s
juries disadvantage racial minorities. Measured
against population, black and white conviction
records diverge by a ratio of about 2.53. But measured
against arrests for the same offenses in the same
counties, the ratio is 0.995—in other words, parity. So

3


whatever produces observed disparities precedes
Florida’s juries.
Third, bigger juries cost more, and costlier juries
are convened less often. Across 200 circuit -year
observations, Florida courts that asked more of their
citizens per trial tried fewer of their cases to juries.
Smaller juries may thereby promote citizen
participation.
Fourth, Petitioner’s own authorities do not show
otherwise. The leading meta -analysis he cites asked
whether jury size changes verdicts and found “no
significant effects.” Michael J. Saks & Mollie
Weighner Marti, A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Jury
Size, 21 L aw & Hum. Behav. 451, 461 (1997) .
Measurements about who sits on juries and how long
they deliberate are not relevant to the core meaning
of a “jury” or whether six jurors get it wrong more
often than twelve.
Empirical evidence does not set  constitutional
meaning. But Petitioner and his amici rely heavily on
empirical assumptions that lack applicability to
Florida’s six-person juries. Six jurors, drawn from the
community and placed between the accused and the
State, supply what original meaning and this Court’s
precedents identify as the jury’s essential feature. The
Court should affirm.

4


ARGUMENT
I. The constitutional significance of the jury
lies principally in its core functions.
“The Constitution itself is silent with respect to a
jury’s proper size.” Kurt D. Engelhardt et al., The Jury
Trial Clause, in The Heritage Guide to the
Constitution 662 (Josh Blackman & John G. Malcolm
eds., 3d ed. 2025). So Petitioner’s constitutional claim
requires that the original meaning of the  “jury”
implicitly include a twelve-person requirement.
Petitioner leads with an attack on  this Court’s
decision in Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970), for
upholding Florida’s six -person jury even while
“acknowledging that the Framers ‘may well’ have had
‘the usual expectation’ in drafting the Sixth
Amendment ‘that the jury would consist of 12’
members.” Pet. Br. 2 (quoting Williams, 399 U.S. at
98–99).
But expected applications are “ relevant only
insofar as [they] can be thought to be reflected in the
understood meaning of the text .” Citizens United  v.
Fed. Election Comm ’n, 558 U.S. 310, 386 (2010)
(Scalia, J., concurring). “[O]riginal meaning”
“controls,” not “expectations about how the text would
apply.” United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 739 n.*
(2024) (Barrett, J., concurring) . In other words,
“[s]pecific expectations about the consequences of a
legal rule are distinct from the meaning of the rule
itself.” Ibid. (quoting Keith E. Whittington,
Originalism: A Critical Introduction , 82 Fordham L.
Rev. 375, 383 (2013)).

5


Thus, evidence that most applications of the jury
right in fact involved twelve jurors does not establish
that the term “jury” itself was unders tood to require
that number. Substantial evidence from all relevant
periods—including around the Sixth Amendment’s
ratification in 1791 and the Fourteenth Amendment’s
ratification in 1868 —suggests that the term “jury”
was principally understood by reference to the body’s
function in the justice system. Cf . New York State
Rifle & Pistol Ass ’n, Inc.  v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 37
(2022) (acknowledging “an ongoing scholarly debate
on whether courts should primarily rely on the
prevailing understanding of an individual right when
the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868
when defining its scope”).
Early dictionaries reflected that petit juries were
“usually” twelve—suggesting that the term “jury” was
not necessarily understood to require that number.
Jury, 2 Noah Webster, An American Dictionary of the
English Language (New York, S. Converse 1828). The
overarching definition was “[a] number of freeholders,
selected in the manner prescribed by law, empaneled
and sworn to inquire into and try any matter of fact,
and to declare the truth on the evidence given them in
the case.”  Ibid.; see also  Jury, Noah Webster,
Webster’s International Dictionary of the English
Language: Being the Authentic Edition of Webster’s
Unabridged Dictionary, Comprising the Issues of
1864, 1879, and 1884, at 806 (London, George Bell &
Sons 1907) (“A body of men, usually twelve, selected
according to law, impaneled and sworn to inquire into
and try any matter of fact, and to render their true
verdict according to the evidence legally adduced.”).

6


So while dictionary definitions explained that the
term “[i]n a narrower sense” meant “ twelve men,
selected and sworn according to law, ” the term more
generally meant “[a] certain number of men, selected
according to law, and sworn  (jurati) to inquire of
certain matters of fact, and declare the truth upon
evidence to be laid before them.” Jury, 2 Alexander M.
Burrill, A Law Dictionary and Glossary  113 ( 2d ed.
New York, John S. Voorhies 1860).
Early legal sources likewise suggest that twelve
was not part of the public understanding of the broad
term “jury.” The Judiciary Act of 1789 was “adopted
by the same Congress that passed the Sixth
Amendment.” Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 100
n.47 (2020); cf. Cohens  v. Virginia, 19 U.S. 264, 420
(1821) (“A contemporaneous exposition of the
constitution . . . is the judiciary act itself.”) ; Sandra
Day O’Connor, The Judiciary Act of 1789 and the
American Judicial Tradition, 59 U. Cin. L. Rev. 1, 3
(1990) (calling the Act “the last of the triad of founding
documents, along with the Declaration of
Independence and the Constitution itself”).
That Act specified that “ in cases punishable with
death, the trial shall be had in the county where the
offence was committed, or where that cannot be done
without great inconvenience, twelve petit jurors at
least shall be summoned from thence .” Judiciary Act
of 1789, ch. 20, § 29, 1 Stat. 73, 88. In all cases, jurors
were to be “ designated by lot or otherwise in each
State respectively according to the mode of forming
juries therein now practised. ” Ibid. The Act
emphasized that Congress did not want “ to incur an
unnecessary expense, or unduly to burthen the

7


citizens of any part of the district with such services.”
Ibid.
Congress thought it necessary to specify that “at
least” “twelve petit” jurors be summoned for capital
cases. If “jury” already meant twelve, the specification
would have been unnecessary. And  Congress did not
specify a number of jurors in other federal criminal
cases; at least “the composition of federal juries varied
both geographically and over time ” based on the
relevant State practices. Ramos, 590 U.S. at 100 n.47.
Participants in the Constitutional Convention
emphasized that “[t]he constitution of Juries is
different in different States .” 2 The Records of the
Federal Convention of 1787, at 628 (Max Farrand ed.,
1911).
The Act’s floor of “at least” twelve in capital cases,
and its silence on  the number otherwise, are hard to
square with the theory that “jury” at the time
inherently meant a body of precisely twelve. And
around 1868, many States allowed juries of fewer than
twelve—while still understanding each set of jurors to
be a “jury.” See, e.g., Mich. Const. of 1850, art. VI, § 28
(“In every criminal prosecution, the accused shall
have the right to a speedy and public trial by an
impartial jury, which may consist of less than twelve
men in all courts not of record . . . .”); Colo. Const. of
1876, art. II, § 23 (similar); Iowa Const. of 1857, art.
I, § 9 (“the general assembly may authorize trial by a
jury of a l ess number than twelve men in inferior
courts”).
When States wanted to address the number of
jurors, they often did so expressly. See M e. Const. of
1820, art. I, § 7 (“The legislature shall provide by law

8


a suitable and impartial mode of selecting juries, and
their usual number and unanimity, in indictments
and convictions, shall be held indispensable.”) ; Cal.
Const. of 1879, art. I, § 7 (“In civil actions, and cases
of misdemeanor, the jury may consist of twelve, or of
any number less than twelve upon which the parties
may agree in open Court.”).
In sum, significant evidence suggests that “jury”
was understood as a broader term about an
institution—a lay body, selected according to law, that
decides facts—rather than implicitly fixing  the
institution’s size.
II. Florida’s six -person juries perform the
jury’s core functions.
If the term “jury” did not inherently require twelve
persons, the question is whether Florida’s six -person
juries satisfy  the core, definitional  functions of the
institution. This Court has said—and Petitioner does
not appear to contest—that “the essential feature of a
jury obviously lies in the interposition between the
accused and his accuser of the commonsense
judgment of a group of laymen, and in the community
participation and shared responsibility that results
from that group’s determination of guilt or innocence.”
Williams, 399 U.S. at 100. The Court thus considered
the effects of smaller juries on outcomes , inc luding
whether there is any “discernible difference between
the results reached by the two different -sized juries.”
Id. at 101. Finding a lack of “evidence” suggesting
such a difference, the Court held that smaller juries
are permissible. Id. at 101–03.

9


Petitioner and his amici try to second -guess this
conclusion as a matter of empirical research, claiming
that “a six-person jury” is “more likely to rule against
a criminal defendant than a jury of 12.” Pet. Br.  30.
Below is an analysis of Florida’s experience, with data
assembled by the Florida State University Institute
for Governance & Civics, that casts doubt on those
claims.1
Data for  Florida’s jury -trial outcomes come from
the circuit criminal chapters of the Florida Office of
the State Courts Administrator ’s annual Trial Court
Statistical Reference Guide; the statewide series
excludes capital murder so that it reflects six -person
juries. Measures of jury burden come from the same
office’s quarterly Jury Management Indices Reports .
The comparisons with larger- jury systems draw on
New York ’s OCA -STAT data for felony cases that
ended in a trial verdict, Washington’s Superior Court
annual criminal caseload reports, and Texas’s fiscal
year 2024 felony case -activity report. The
demographic analyses use ten -year conviction
extracts from the Florida Department of Corrections ;
arrest and conviction data from the  Florida
Department of Law Enforcement’s Criminal Justice
Data Transparency program ; and census-derived

modes, and selection into trial differ across these
systems, the cross- state comparisons provide sound
descriptive evidence but do not show causation.
This analysis suggests that  Florida’s six -person
juries regularly reject the prosecution’s case, at rates
above several larger-jury benchmarks. The available
data do not identify six -person juries as the source of

11


observed racial disparities. Smaller juries make jury
trials less costly to provide, and less costly jury trials
are associated with greater jury  use. And the studies
Petitioner relies on do not show that six-person juries
disadvantage defendants.
A. Florida juries regularly reject the
prosecution’s case.
To begin, Florida juries regularly reject
prosecution positions , so six -person juries are not
producing near- automatic convictions.  Analyzing
noncapital Florida outcomes from fiscal years 2020–
21 through 2024–25 (excluding guilty pleas entered
after trial began ), prosecutions were rejected —
through either acquittal or dismissal —at a rate of
about 27.7%. The rate held between 27.0% and 28.5%
every year, with no statistically significant year -toyear variation. Thus, this finding is not an artifact of
one anomalous period.
The Florida result is also geographically broad, not
the product of a few atypical counties. 3 Sixteen of the
twenty circuits exceed a 20% rejection rate, and
nineteen exceed 15%. Removing any single circuit —
Miami-Dade, Broward, Orange, or any other—shifts
the statewide rate by no more than 1.1 percentage
points. So a robust prosecution rejection rate reflect s
the operation of the Florida system generally.
The result holds across offense categories as well.
Over the three most recent years,  rejection rates ran
roughly 17 –20% for noncapital murder, 23 –26% for


3 The circuit-level data include a small number of capital cases,
which involve twelve-person juries.

12


sexual offenses, 21 –26% for drugs, and 35 –38% for
other crimes against persons.
Another way to analyze Florida’s experience is to
consider similar States with larger -jury
requirements. Those States ca n provide helpful
empirical benchmarks , albeit not  causal natural
experiments.
Start with New York , which  uses twelve -person
juries. In New York felony cases arraigned from 2021
through 2024 that ended in a trial verdict,  20.2%
ended in acquittal . New York combines jury and
bench verdicts, and does not separately report
dismissals. Because Florida’s figure includes
dismissals and New York’s does not, the two rates
cannot be precisely ranked against each other. What
the New York data show is that a twelve- person
system acquits in roughly one felony verdict in five —
a rate that does not  show a  defendant-protection
superiority over Florida.
The same is true of Washington, which has an
acquittal rate of about 21.2% in the predominantly
larger-jury Superior Court between 2021 and 2025
(excluding King County, whose data are unavailable).
Again, the statistics are slightly different, as
Washington combines jury, nonjury, and stipulated
outcomes, but the point is similar.
Likewise, in fiscal year 2024, Texas felony juries
returned 473 acquittals in 2,162 verdicts —a 21.9%
rate. Once again, the comparison is not exact: Texas’s
statewide source combines district  courts (where
juries are twelve) and statutory county courts  (where

13


juries can be smaller). But district courts, which seat
twelve, generally try Texas felonies.4
These larger-jury benchmarks suggest that
Florida’s six -person system does not produce an
obviously less defendant -protective pattern.  A jury
that repeatedly rejects prosecution positions across
years, circuits, and offenses is functioning as a
genuine intermediary between government and
accused. The comparative evidence gives no sign that
jurors seven through twelve supply measurable
protection for defendants. Thus, if the constitutional
concern is preservation of the jury’s protective
function, contemporary evidence does not
demonstrate that twelve is necessary to secure that
function.
B. Observed demographic disparities do not
identify Florida ’s six -person juries as
their source.
A distinct question could be  whether minority
defendants are disadvantaged by Florida’s juries .
Petitioner dwells on this question, even though the
original understanding of “jury” does not appear to
focus on it. And this Court has refused to indulge the
assumption that a juror “would be partial to the
defendant because of their shared race.” Flowers v.
Mississippi, 588 U.S. 284, 299 (2019) (quoting Batson
v. Kentucky, 476 U.S. 79, 97  (1986)). Petitioner’s
argument appears to depend on this rejected
assumption. See Pet. Br.  33 (claiming that


4 See Texas Judicial Branch, About Texas Courts,
https://perma.cc/8T83-4JZ6.

14


“increas[ing] black representation ” will “ make trial
outcomes more equal for white and black
defendants”). Plus, “[d]efendants are not entitled to a
jury of any particular composition.” Holland  v.
Illinois, 493 U.S. 474, 483 (1990).
Of course, Williams recognized that a jury  should
be large enough “ to provide a fair possibility for
obtaining a representative[] cross -section of the
community.” 399 U.S. at 100 . And a s a theoretical
matter, larger juries—including juries with more than
twelve people—are mechanically more likely to
contain members of minority groups. But composition
probabilities and defendant outcomes are distinct
empirical questions.
Here, though data are limited, the  black-white
conviction-record ratio relative to population (and
adjusted for county and offense category)  is about
2.53. But that ratio becomes  0.995 when normalized
by race-specific arrests for the  same offenses in the
same countie s. A value of 1 represents aggregate
parity, so this result indicates that most of the
population-based racial disparity is present before the
conviction stage . This ratio remained near 1 when
minimum sample -size requirements were changed,
and when individual counties or offense categories
were removed, suggesting a relatively robust
measure. The available data therefore do not identify
Florida’s six-person jury rule as the source of observed
racial disparities.

15


C. Jury size bears on the availability of
citizen adjudication.
The jury right reflects an  “insistence upon
community participation in the determination of guilt
or innocence.” Duncan v. Louisiana, 391 U.S. 145, 156
(1968). “The opportunity for ordinary citizens to
participate in the administration of justice has long
been recognized as one of the principal justifications
for retaining the jury system.” Powers v. Ohio, 499
U.S. 400, 406 (1991) . But a  jury right that becomes
materially more burdensome to invoke can reduce
actual citizen participation.
Twelve-person juries inherently require
substantially greater citizen inputs than six -person
ones. The Florida Supreme Court’s jury-management
goals provide a benchmark of  18.3 prospective jurors
brought in for six -person trial s and 30.5 for twelve -
person trials—about two-thirds more.5
Florida’s data also associate heavier jury burdens
with less jury use. The State’ s jury -management
reports span twenty judicial circuits over ten fiscal
years—200 circuit -year observations.  Setting aside
the pandemic-disrupted years, circuits that brought in
more people per trial tried a smaller share of their
criminal cases to juries. The relationship is
proportional and statistically significant. Controlling
for circuit and year, a 10% increase in people brought
in per trial is associated with about 2.4% less jury use.


5 Fla. Off. of the State Cts. Adm ’r, Jury Management Indices
Report 1 (quarter ending Dec. 31, 2025) , https://perma.cc/8JDC-
66NY.

16


And because twelve- person trials call for about two -
thirds more prospective jurors than six -person trials,
this estimate suggests that a twelve-person mandate
could mean noticeably fewer jury trials —and fewer
occasions for ordinary citizens “to participate in the
administration of justice.” Powers, 499 U.S. at 406.6
In sum, Florida’s six-person jury rule preserves the
jury’s check on prosecutors  while lowering the
institutional cost of providing juries. In that way,
Florida’s rule  appears to  advance, rather than
undermine, the historical function of adjudication by
citizen juries.
D. Petitioner’s empirical evidence does not
show that Florida’s system disadvantages
defendants.
Petitioner and his amici  invoke empirical studies
for four distinct propositions: (1) larger juries are
more likely to include minorities; (2) larger juries
deliberate differently; (3) those differences make
verdicts more accurate; and (4) six -person criminal
juries therefore produce worse outcomes for
defendants. The evidence gets progressively weaker
as one moves down that cha in. And much of the
available literature relies on experiments, civil juries,
process measures, or modeled implications rather


6 The underlying Florida management measures combine six -
and twelve -person proceedings, so the  data cannot isolate the
effect of jury  size. The closest  proxy—the average number of
prospective jurors per voir -dire panel —is not significantly
related to jury-trial rates in these data.

17


than contemporary six -versus-twelve criminaloutcome comparisons.
Starting with the first proposition, there is no
question that a larger random sample is more likely
to include members of a minority group. So a random
sample of eighteen  people is more likely to  include
more members of a minority group than a sample of
twelve. But this says nothing about verdicts. The
study Petitioner and his amici rely on here finds that
representation in actual trials is “not significantly
different from the predicted proportions from a
random draw.” Shari Seidman Diamond et al.,
Achieving Diversity on the Jury: Jury Size and the
Peremptory Challenge, 6 J. Empirical Legal Stud. 425,
445 (2009) (cited at Pet. Br.  33). That study  says
nothing about how jury size affects verdicts, much less
criminal ones—it considered civil trials in which “the
assignment of cases” to juries of different sizes “ was
not random.” Id. at 434, 444 n.63. Nor can the study
explain, even assuming that some undefined level of
“greater heterogeneity” is part of the original meaning
of “jury,” Pet. Br. 33, why courts or States can stop at
twelve jurors.
Next, Petitioner and his amici  rely on a study of
felony trials in two Florida counties finding a black -
white conviction gap that was eliminated when the
jury pool included at least one black prospective juror.
Shamena Anwar et al., The Impact of Jury Race in
Criminal Trials, 127 Q.J. Econ. 1017 , 1019 (2012)
(cited at Pet. Br.  33). The study held  jury size
constant, excluding Florida’s twelve -person capital
juries and focusing instead on venire composition. See
id. at 1024–25, 1027. So it cannot provide direct

18


evidence about the effect of increasing the number of
seated jurors on  outcomes. The sentence Petitioner
relies on from this study —that “[i ]ncreasing the
number of jurors on the seated jury woul d . . . make
trial outcomes more equal ”—is a policy proposal  by
the authors, not a finding. Id. at 1049. The study does
not support Petitioner’s proposed chain from jury size
to minority representation to  racial outcome
disparity.
Last, Petitioner and his amici rely on a 1997 metaanalysis of prior studies . Michael J. Saks & Mollie
Weighner Marti, A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Jury
Size, 21 Law & Hum. Behav. 451 (1997) . Petitioner
uses this analysis to suggest that twelve-person juries
“deliberate longer,” Pet. Br. 34, but the analysis itself
notes that “process ineffic iencies associated with
greater numbers of decision -makers” could explain
any difference —and that the observed “mean time
difference is not great.” Saks & Marti , supra, at 458.
More importantly, the analysis found “no significant
effects” on the accuracy of verdicts, in the sense of “the
best available estimation of what the full community
would decide regarding that trial.” Id . at 461. Thus,
this analysis does not support the proposition that
twelve-person juries produce more accurate verdicts,
fewer wrongful convictions, or lower conviction rates
than six-person ones.
* * *
A jury of twelve has a historical pedigree.  But if a
twelve-person requirement is not specifically part of
the original public meaning of the “jury,” Florida ’s
smaller juries fit the jury ’s purpose as an institution
of lay judgment and checking power. None of this is to

19


suggest that these types of  empirical analyses “shed
light on the meaning of the Constitution .” Dobbs v.
Jackson Women ’s Health Org. , 597 U.S. 215, 273
(2022). Rather, e mpirical evidence can test
Petitioner’s claims about the institutional function of
the jury, assessing whether Florida’s juries match the
core constitutional meaning. And t he available
evidence does not show functional failure in Florida .
It shows Florida ’s juries rejecting the prosecution ’s
case at a substantial and steady rate across circuits
and offense categories —at rates above  larger-jury
benchmarks in other States.
CONCLUSION
For these reasons, the Court should affirm.
